cells.speakerNotes: Welcome! We're really excited to be here today.

I'm Tobias, and this is my co-presenter Gerald.

We're both employee-owners of Caktus Group, a small Django development company based in North Carolina.

I'm a developer and devops person, and Gerald leads quality assurance for Caktus.

We had a lot of help with this presentation from our colleagues Colin and Simon, who helped with working out the slides and the initial implementation for our client, respectively.

To set the stage today, we need to take a step back and talk about criminal record expungement.

(Tobias) For this section of the presentation I will hand it off to Gerald.

(Gerald) This is an area of legal aid where non-profit organizations, public defenders,
and sometimes private attorneys help community members clear eligible charges
from their records, such as dismissed or not guilty charges. ( One thing that some people may not realize is that a not guilty or dismissed charge can still show on a person's record)

So for someone trying to secure housing or apply for a job, an expungement can
be life-changing. 
But under the hood, the process of preparing these petitions for expungements
is painfully manual. 
Attorneys and paralegals must track down potentially hundreds of records spanning decades—review every single charge, then manually enter everything into strictly formatted court forms.

So here's an overview of what the full process looks like.

Everything starts with intake.  When a client comes in looking for expungement, staff needs to
collect every name the client has gone by, their date of birth....and the counties they've lived in, so nothing gets missed in the record search that follows.

Once all the data is collected from a client, it's time to search. This is the step we're focused on today!
Staff then have to search court and
law-enforcement databases for every record tied to that client. 
This is where things can get tricky because names are sometimes typed or written inconsistently; there could be misspellings, nicknames, or abbreviations ( such as Matt instead of Matthew)
So a simple exact-match search will miss records that exist in those databases.

Once every record is found for a client, each charge gets checked against state
statutes to see if it qualifies for expungement.

From there, every eligible charge has to be transcribed onto strictly
formatted court petition forms, by hand, which is  another
manual, error-prone step in this process.

Finally, the completed petition is filed with the court. If it's
granted, the records are cleared — but getting here can take weeks of
manual work for a single client.

When we first took on this project, we assumed the main challenges would be things like eligibility mapping, applying North Carolina statutes, and cleanly inserting them into standardized court forms. But that changed once we held a dedicated discovery workshop with the client.

During the workshop, we realized that finding the proper records
"quickly" was the true bottleneck preventing eligible community
members from getting help.

Thorough record checks are critical because conviction expunctions in North Carolina are generally a one-shot opportunity. 
Once a court grants a conviction expunction, the client cannot use that statute again. This means any omitted conviction stays on their record permanently. 
Running a comprehensive statewide search is essential to make sure no eligible charges are missed before filing.

Here is the core problem: the state transitioned away from its legacy system
to a "modern" web portal. While you might expect a newer system to speed up
legal workflows, in reality, it severely restricted how attorneys can search
for records.

Pause to play video

As you can see on screen, doing a simple name search in this portal routinely
takes 10 to 15 seconds—or longer—per query. In our discovery workshop with the
client, staff shared that under the new portal system, their record-pulling time
grew from 3 hours up to 10 hours per client.

To make matters worse, while the
system does claim to offer fuzzy search matching, the underlying logic is poorly
implemented; it balloons a tight 6-item result into over 200 useless matches, which are mostly false positives. Rather than giving attorneys what they actually need.

So why is finding everyone so hard? In our case, we were dealing with a
database of over 50 million North Carolina court records, and searching by
name in a dataset that size is not easy.

We're not just looking for a "single" record. We're looking for every
record that belongs to a single person.

Secondly, if you think about the lifespan of a criminal record, one can imagine how
frequent typos can be.
"A name gets typed on the side of the road by an arresting officer. It gets transcribed from a handwritten form by a rushed court clerk. Or it’s provided by a client who uses nicknames, hyphenated names, or spells their name differently across legal documents."

On top of that, name collisions are everywhere—thousands of people share the
exact same first and last name. And date of birth—the one field that could
easily disambiguate two people—is sometimes missing in court data.

We realized that if we wanted to build a tool that truly served legal aid
organizations, public defenders, and community advocates, we had to solve
this multi-million record fuzzy search problem using our tools of choice,
which are.......Django and PostgreSQL.

To talk more about that, I'll hand it off to Tobias.

To help understand the scope of the problem and some of the assumptions we as programmers and technologists might make about names, we highly recommend the article linked here, "Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names," by Patrick McKenzie in 2010.

Some of them are pretty funny, and I recommend reading through them all on your own time.

To share just 5 of the 40,

one is that people have exactly one name. In reality, they may have multiple aliases, spellings, nicknames that they use regularly.
Another is that names often change over time, through marriage, divorce, or simply deciding to change one's name.

Another is that people have a different first name and last name --and this hits close to home with Django's User model--that they have a first name and last name at all. In other countries and cultures, names often don't fit into the neat "first name" and "last name" boxes.

Another assumption is that names are written in ASCII.

In our case, the entire database of 54 million plus court records was written in ASCII, so non-ASCII characters were simply not present in our dataset.

Finally--and this one is was also abundant on our project--it's easy to assume that names will be typed exactly and perfectly every time they're entered. This is not the case, and our dataset of 54M records provided ample evidence of this.

In production, the data is purchased from the North Carolina court system. For testing purposes, we generated a fake dataset that loosely matched the shape of the production data:

- Sourced from ~1,000,000 last names and ~600,000 first names from Kaggle
- Names are randomly weighted according to their precedence in the United States
- Combined and assigned a random birth date
- Each name appears from 1-80 times in the database, and has some typos injected

The data dump we receive from the stateis NOT a clean, unified "Person" table. It is a list of
raw court records. Every time a person's name gets entered into the
courts — different county, different clerk, different year — a new row is
created. So the same real person shows up across many duplicated records,
often with typos, nicknames, and aliases.

This is loosely what the data model looks, with a first name, last name, middle name, and date of birth field.

We added the person_id field for demonstration purposes to help us see if we tracked down all the records corresponding to that person or not.

That duplication is exactly why the search is hard: "Amanda Morgan" is
not one row we look up; it is a cluster of rows we have to find and
de-duplicate.
To help
For example

In summary, this is a hard problem! There is no magical combination of these algorithms that will solve all your search issues.

Our goal with this project was to fine tune the a particular set of algoirthms, and enable our users to with a search that is super fast so they can quickly try different combinations or nicknames to find the cases they're looking for.

And the fact the postgres can do this on my 3 year old laptop is awesome!
